sections.text:
Joel begins with a plague of locusts that has stripped the land. He reads it as a warning of the day of the LORD and calls everyone, from priests to children, to return to God with their whole heart.

God answers with a promise to restore what the locusts have eaten, and beyond that to pour out his Spirit on all people, young and old, men and women.
The book gives no date and names no king, so proposals range over several centuries. Joel is one of the twelve shorter prophetic books that Jewish tradition counts together as one scroll.

On the day of Pentecost, Peter explains what is happening by quoting Joel’s promise of the Spirit (Acts 2). Christians therefore read that promise as fulfilled in the church. The day of the LORD in the prophets is both judgment and rescue, and Joel holds the two together.
